## Importance of Univariate Data Visualization

Univariate data visualization allows the for the isolation of a single variable to be analyzed to determine how each variable interacts with other variables or what messages can be gathered from the single variable (Volckens, 2024). Univariate data visualization can help with the creation of new variables or features. 
Creating Visualizations of the data helps with identifying patterns such as normality, skewness, and or uniformity in the data. Univariate data visualization allows for the detection of outliers and run quick central tendency assessments. 




```{r Crime.Status Bar Chart-Cat, echo=FALSE}
crime |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Status)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = Status), color = "black")
```

Note that the `echo = FALSE` parameter was added to the code chunk to prevent printing of the R code that generated the plot.

```{r Crime.AREA.NAME Bar Chart-Cat, echo=FALSE}
crime |>
  ggplot(aes(x = AREA.NAME)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = AREA.NAME), color = "black")+
  theme(axis.title.x=element_blank(),
        axis.text.x=element_blank(),
        axis.ticks.x=element_blank())
```

```{r Crime.Vict.Desc Bar Chart-Cat, echo=FALSE}
crime |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Vict.Descent)) +
  geom_bar(aes(fill = Vict.Descent), color = "black")
```


``` {r Crime.VIC.AGE Histogram-Quant}
# Create a histogram for years of education
crime |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Vict.Age)) +
  # Change the number of bins, fill shading, and outline color
  # Colors may be listed by name ("Purple") or in hex format ("#1f77b4")
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, fill = "#9467bd", color = "black") +
  # Add axis labels
  labs(x = "Victim Age", y = "Count")

```

``` {r Crime.VIC.AGE Boxplot-Quant}
# Create a box plot for years
crime |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Vict.Age)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#17becf", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Age of Victims")

```

``` {r Crime.VICT.AGE Density-Quant}

# Create a density plot for years
crime |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Vict.Age)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#1f77b4", color = "black") +
  labs(x = "Age of Victims", y = "Density")

```

``` {r Crime.VIC.AGE Probably Plot}

# plotting data with proper labels 
# And adding line with proper properties
qqplot <- ggplot(crime, aes(sample = Vict.Age)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "blue") +
  ggtitle("Normal Probability Plot of Victim Age") +
  theme_minimal()

# Display the plot
print(qqplot)

```
``` {r 4 plot for Crime.Vict.Age}


# Create plots
p1 <- ggplot(crime, aes(x = Crm.Cd.1, y = Vict.Age)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue") +
  ggtitle("Run")

p2 <- ggplot(crime, aes(x = Vict.Age)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "blue", color = "black", bins = 30) +
  ggtitle("Histogram")

p3 <- ggplot(crime, aes(x = dplyr::lag(Vict.Age), y = Vict.Age)) +
  geom_point(color = "red") +
  ggtitle("Lag Plot")

p4 <- ggplot(crime, aes(sample = scale(Vict.Age))) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line(color = "red") +
  ggtitle("Normal Probability Plot")

# Arrange the plots in a 2x2 grid
grid.arrange(p1, p2, p3, p4, ncol = 2)
```
